concepts: Quadratic equation with real coefficients: nature of roots
Complex number as a root of a real quadratic
questions.question: Let $z$ be a complex number such that the imaginary part of $z$ is nonzero and $a=z^2+z+1$ is real. Then $a$ cannot take the value: [JEE-2012]
questions.key_idea: A real quadratic has non-real roots only when its discriminant is negative.
solution: $z^2+z+1-a=0$ is a quadratic in $z$ with real coefficients (since $a$ is real).
Hence $z=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{4a-3}}{2}$.
$z$ must have non-zero imaginary part, so $\sqrt{4a-3}$ must be imaginary: $4a-3<0$, i.e. $a<\frac34$.
If $a=\frac34$ then $z=-\frac12$ is purely real, and if $a>\frac34$ both roots are real; so $a=\frac34$ (or any $a\ge\frac34$) is impossible.
The values $-1,\ \frac13,\ \frac12$ are all less than $\frac34$, so they are possible; $\frac34$ is not.
So $a$ cannot take the value $\frac34$: option (D).
questions.correction_note: PDF only says 'a != 3/4, otherwise z will be purely real'. The exact condition for non-real z is 4a-3<0, i.e. a<3/4 (a>3/4 also gives real roots); the answer D is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $z=x+iy$ and make the imaginary part of $a$ zero: this forces $x=-\frac12$ and gives $a=\frac34-y^2$.
solution: $a$ is real, so $y(2x+1)=0$; as $y\neq0$ we get $x=-\frac12$.
Then $a=\frac14-y^2-\frac12+1=\frac34-y^2$.
Since $y\neq0$, $y^2>0$, so $a<\frac34$ strictly.
The option $\frac34$ would need $y=0$, which is excluded: $a$ cannot be $\frac34$.

useful_results: For real $b,c$: $z^2+bz+c$ is real for a non-real $z$ exactly when $\mathrm{Re}\,z=-\frac b2$ (imaginary part is $y(2x+b)$).
Then the value is $c-\frac{b^2}{4}-y^2$: every real value below the vertex value $c-\frac{b^2}{4}$ is attained by some non-real $z$, and nothing else is.
Here $b=c=1$: attainable values are exactly $a<\frac34$ (check $a=0$: $z=\frac{-1\pm i\sqrt3}{2}$, and indeed $z^2+z+1=0$).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Roots of unity on the unit circle
Half-planes in the Argand plane and angle between position vectors
questions.question: Let $w=\frac{\sqrt3+i}{2}$ and $P=\{w^n:n=1,2,3,\dots\}$. Further $H_1=\left\{z\in C:\mathrm{Re}\,z>\frac12\right\}$ and $H_2=\left\{z\in C:\mathrm{Re}\,z<\frac{-1}{2}\right\}$, where $C$ is the set of all complex numbers. If $z_1\in P\cap H_1$, $z_2\in P\cap H_2$ and $O$ represents the origin, then $\angle z_1Oz_2=$ [JEE-Adv.2013]
questions.key_idea: $P$ is the set of 12th roots of unity, so only multiples of $30^\circ$ matter; $\mathrm{Re}\,z=\cos\theta$ picks the points.
solution: $w=\cos\frac\pi6+i\sin\frac\pi6$, so $P=\{w^n\}=\left\{\cos\frac{n\pi}{6}+i\sin\frac{n\pi}{6}\right\}$: the 12 points on the unit circle at angles that are multiples of $30^\circ$.
$H_1$: $\mathrm{Re}\,z=\cos\frac{n\pi}6>\frac12$ holds only for angles $\pm30^\circ$ (at $\pm60^\circ$ the real part is exactly $\frac12$, not greater).
So $z_1=\frac{\sqrt3+i}{2}$ or $\frac{\sqrt3-i}{2}$.
$H_2$: $\cos\frac{n\pi}6<-\frac12$ holds for angles $150^\circ,180^\circ,210^\circ$.
So $z_2=\frac{-\sqrt3+i}{2},\ -1$ or $\frac{-\sqrt3-i}{2}$.
Angle between $z_1$ (at $30^\circ$) and $z_2$ (at $150^\circ,180^\circ,210^\circ$) is $120^\circ,150^\circ,180^\circ$; $z_1$ at $-30^\circ$ gives the same set by symmetry.
Hence $\angle z_1Oz_2\in\left\{\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{6},\pi\right\}$, so options (C) and (D) are possible.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with exponents: $z_2/z_1=w^{m-n}$ and the angle is $30^\circ\times$ the circular distance between the exponents mod 12.
solution: Index the points by $n\in\{1,\dots,12\}$ (angle $30^\circ n$). $\mathrm{Re}\,w^n>\frac12\iff\cos(30^\circ n)>\frac12\iff n\equiv\pm1\pmod{12}$.
$\mathrm{Re}\,w^m<-\frac12\iff n\in\{5,6,7\}$ (angles $150^\circ,180^\circ,210^\circ$).
$z_1=w^{n}$, $n\in\{1,11\}$ and $z_2=w^{m}$, $m\in\{5,6,7\}$; the angle at $O$ equals $30^\circ\cdot\min(|m-n|,\,12-|m-n|)$.
The possible angles are $\frac{2\pi}3,\frac{5\pi}{6},\pi$: options (C) and (D).

useful_results: On the unit circle $\mathrm{Re}\,z=\cos\theta$, so a condition like $\mathrm{Re}\,z>c$ is just an arc $|\theta|<\cos^{-1}c$: count the $N$th roots of unity on the arc by the spacing $\frac{2\pi}{N}$.
The angle between $e^{i\theta_1}$ and $e^{i\theta_2}$ is $\min(|\theta_1-\theta_2|,\,2\pi-|\theta_1-\theta_2|)\in[0,\pi]$; for $N$th roots of unity use exponent differences mod $N$.
Beware strict vs non-strict inequalities: here $\cos60^\circ=\frac12$ is excluded from $H_1$, which removes $e^{\pm i\pi/3}$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Cube roots of unity: sums of powers
Matrix product and rank-one matrices
questions.question: Let $\omega$ be a complex cube root of unity with $\omega\neq1$ and $P=[p_{ij}]$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with $p_{ij}=\omega^{i+j}$. Then $P^2\neq0$, when $n=$ [JEE-Adv.2013]
questions.key_idea: Each entry of $P^2$ factors as $\omega^{i+j}\sum_{k=1}^n\omega^{2k}$, and that sum vanishes exactly when $3\mid n$.
solution: $P^2=[\alpha_{ij}]_{n\times n}$ with $\alpha_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}p_{ik}\,p_{kj}$.
$\alpha_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^n\omega^{i+k}\cdot\omega^{k+j}=\omega^{i+j}\sum_{k=1}^n\omega^{2k}$.
So $\alpha_{ij}=\omega^{i+j}\left(\omega^2+\omega^4+\omega^6+\dots+\omega^{2n}\right)$.
If $n$ is a multiple of 3, the terms group in threes $\omega^2+\omega^4+\omega^6=\omega^2+\omega+1=0$, so the sum is $0$ and $P^2=0$.
Hence $P^2\neq0\iff 3\nmid n$.
$57=3\times19$ is a multiple of 3; $55,58,56$ are not. So $n=55,58,56$: options (B), (C), (D).
questions.correction_note: PDF shows only 'if n is a multiple of 3 then P^2=0, so n is not a multiple of 3', which proves one direction. The converse (the sum is non-zero when 3 does not divide n, so P^2 != 0) was added using the GP formula. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $P=uu^{T}$ with $u=(\omega,\omega^2,\dots,\omega^n)^{T}$ has rank one, so $P^2=(u^{T}u)\,P$.
solution: $p_{ij}=\omega^i\omega^j$, so $P=uu^{T}$ where $u=(\omega,\omega^2,\dots,\omega^n)^{T}$ (a column vector).
$P^2=u\,(u^{T}u)\,u^{T}=(u^{T}u)\,P$, where $u^{T}u=\sum_{k=1}^n\omega^{2k}$ is a scalar.
$P\neq0$ (its entries have modulus 1), so $P^2=0\iff u^{T}u=\sum_{k=1}^n\omega^{2k}=0$.
$\sum_{k=1}^n\omega^{2k}$ cycles through partial sums $\omega^2,\ \omega^2+\omega,\ 0$ (for $n\equiv1,2,0\pmod3$), i.e. $\omega^2,\,-1,\,0$.
So $P^2\neq0$ exactly when $3\nmid n$: $n=55,58,56$.

useful_results: For column vectors $u,v$: $(uv^{T})^2=(v^{T}u)\,uv^{T}$. A rank-one matrix squares to a scalar multiple of itself, and it is nilpotent exactly when $v^{T}u=0$.
$\sum_{k=1}^n\omega^k$ equals $0$ if $3\mid n$, $\omega$ if $n\equiv1$, and $-1$ if $n\equiv2\pmod3$ (and the same pattern for $\omega^{2k}$ with $\omega^2$ replacing $\omega$); check $n=1,2,3$.
Matrices built from $p_{ij}=f(i)g(j)$ are rank one: look for this before multiplying out.

concepts: Loci in the Argand plane: disc, half-plane and sector
Area of a circular sector
questions.paragraph: Let $S=S_1\cap S_2\cap S_3$, where $S_1=\{z\in C:|z|<4\}$, $S_2=\left\{z\in C:\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{z-1+\sqrt3i}{1-\sqrt3i}\right]>0\right\}$ and $S_3=\{z\in C:\mathrm{Re}\,z>0\}$.
questions.question: Area of $S=$ [JEE-Adv.2013]
questions.key_idea: $\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{z-z_0}{c}\right]>0$ is a half-plane bounded by a line through $z_0$; here that line passes through the origin.
solution: $S_1$ is the interior of the circle with centre at the origin and radius $4$.
$S_3$: $\mathrm{Re}\,z>0$ is the right half-plane (first and fourth quadrants).
For $S_2$ put $z=x+iy$: $\frac{z-1+\sqrt3i}{1-\sqrt3i}=\frac{\left[(x-1)+i\left(y+\sqrt3\right)\right]\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)}{4}$.
Its imaginary part is $\frac{\sqrt3(x-1)+\left(y+\sqrt3\right)}{4}=\frac{\sqrt3x+y}{4}$, so $S_2$ is $\sqrt3x+y>0$.
The line $\sqrt3x+y=0$ passes through the origin at $-60^\circ$ to the $x$-axis; $S_2$ is the side containing $(1,0)$.
$S$ is therefore the part of the disc of radius 4 with polar angle from $-60^\circ$ to $90^\circ$: a sector of angle $150^\circ=\frac{5\pi}{6}$.
Area $=\frac12(4)^2\cdot\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{20\pi}{3}$ (equivalently quarter disc $\frac{\pi(4)^2}{4}=4\pi$ plus a $60^\circ$ sector $\frac12(4)^2\frac\pi3=\frac{8\pi}{3}$).
questions.correction_note: PDF says S1 is centred at (0,1) (it is centred at the origin: |z|<4), expands the numerator as (x-1)+i(y-sqrt3) (it should be i(y+sqrt3)) with denominator 2 (it is 4), and later mentions the point (1,-3) (the line through (1,-sqrt3) is meant). The line sqrt3 x + y = 0 and the area 20pi/3 are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the argument: $\mathrm{Im}\,\frac{z-z_0}{c}>0\iff\arg\frac{z-z_0}{c}\in(0,\pi)$, so $S_2$ is a half-plane read off from angles.
solution: $1-\sqrt3i=2e^{-i\pi/3}$, and $z-\left(1-\sqrt3i\right)$ is the vector from $A=\left(1,-\sqrt3\right)$ to $z$; note $A=2e^{-i\pi/3}$ lies on the ray at $-60^\circ$ through the origin.
$\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{z-A}{2e^{-i\pi/3}}\right]>0\iff\arg(z-A)+\frac\pi3\in(0,\pi)\iff\arg(z-A)\in\left(-\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$.
That is the open half-plane bounded by the line through $A$ in direction $-60^\circ$, i.e. the line through the origin and $A$, on the left of that direction.
Together with $\mathrm{Re}\,z>0$ and $|z|<4$, $S$ is the sector of angles $\left(-\frac\pi3,\frac\pi2\right)$, of angle $\frac{5\pi}{6}$.
Area $=\frac12r^2\theta=\frac12\cdot16\cdot\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{20\pi}{3}$.

useful_results: $\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{z-a}{b}\right]>0$ describes the open half-plane bounded by the line through $a$ in the direction of $b$ (the line $\mathrm{Im}\,\frac{z-a}{b}=0$); the side is found by testing one point.
Area of a circular sector of radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ (radians) is $\frac12r^2\theta$; a region cut from a disc by lines through the centre is a sector.
Check of the instance: $\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{z-1+\sqrt3 i}{1-\sqrt3i}\right]=\frac{\sqrt3x+y}{4}$; at $z=1$ it is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}>0$.

concepts: Loci in the Argand plane: distance from a point to a region
Distance of a point from a line
questions.paragraph: Let $S=S_1\cap S_2\cap S_3$, where $S_1=\{z\in C:|z|<4\}$, $S_2=\left\{z\in C:\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{z-1+\sqrt3i}{1-\sqrt3i}\right]>0\right\}$ and $S_3=\{z\in C:\mathrm{Re}\,z>0\}$.
questions.question: $\min_{z\in S}|1-3i-z|=$ [JEE-Adv.2013]
questions.key_idea: $|z-(1-3i)|$ is the distance from $A=(1,-3)$; the nearest point of $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular to the boundary line, provided it lies in $S$.
solution: $|1-3i-z|=|z-(1-3i)|$ is the distance of $z$ from the point $A=(1,-3)$.
$A$ gives $\sqrt3(1)+(-3)=\sqrt3-3<0$, so $A$ lies outside $S_2$, on the other side of the line $L:\ \sqrt3x+y=0$.
So the nearest point of $S$ to $A$ is on the boundary $L$: the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $A$ to $L$ (if $F$ belongs to the closure of $S$).
Along $L$ with unit direction $\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ the foot is at distance $A\cdot\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\frac{1+3\sqrt3}{2}\approx3.10$ from $O$.
$3.10<4$ and the $x$-coordinate $\frac{1+3\sqrt3}{4}>0$, so $F$ lies in the closure of $S$ (on its boundary).
Distance $AF=\frac{\left|\sqrt3\cdot1+(-3)\right|}{\sqrt{3+1}}=\frac{3-\sqrt3}{2}$, approached by points of $S$ next to $F$ (the minimum of the closure).
So $\min|1-3i-z|=\frac{3-\sqrt3}{2}$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the boundary line and minimise the squared distance as a quadratic in the parameter.
solution: Points of $L$: $(t,-\sqrt3t)$. Squared distance to $A=(1,-3)$: $f(t)=(t-1)^2+\left(3-\sqrt3t\right)^2=4t^2-\left(2+6\sqrt3\right)t+10$.
The vertex is at $t=\frac{2+6\sqrt3}{8}=\frac{1+3\sqrt3}{4}\approx1.55$, which gives a point with $x>0$ and $|z|=2t\approx3.10<4$: inside the allowed region.
$\left(\frac{3-\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2=\frac{12-6\sqrt3}{4}=3-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$, so the minimum distance is $\frac{3-\sqrt3}{2}$.

useful_results: Distance from a point to a convex region: if the point is outside, the nearest point is on the boundary; take the perpendicular foot to the nearest side and check it lies inside the other constraints (here $|z|<4$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,z>0$).
Distance of $(x_1,y_1)$ from $ax+by+c=0$ is $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$.
A strict inequality makes the minimum an infimum (not attained); in MCQs one still reports it as the minimum value.

concepts: Circles in the Argand plane
Inversion in the unit circle and modulus algebra
questions.question: Let complex numbers $\alpha$ and $\frac1{\bar\alpha}$ lie on circles $(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2=r^2$ and $(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2=4r^2$, respectively. If $z_0=x_0+iy_0$ satisfies the equation $2|z_0|^2=r^2+2$, then $|\alpha|=$ [JEE-Adv.2013]
questions.key_idea: Square both circle conditions and eliminate the cross term $\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0$ between them.
solution: $\alpha$ lies on the first circle and $\frac1{\bar\alpha}$ on the second: $|\alpha-z_0|=r$ and $\left|\frac1{\bar\alpha}-z_0\right|=2r$.
Squaring the first: $(\alpha-z_0)(\bar\alpha-\bar z_0)=r^2\Rightarrow|\alpha|^2-\alpha\bar z_0-\bar\alpha z_0+|z_0|^2=r^2$ ... (i)
Since $\frac1{\bar\alpha}=\frac{\alpha}{|\alpha|^2}$, the second gives $\left(\frac{\alpha}{|\alpha|^2}-z_0\right)\left(\frac{\bar\alpha}{|\alpha|^2}-\bar z_0\right)=4r^2$.

Expanding: $\frac1{|\alpha|^2}-\frac{\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0}{|\alpha|^2}+|z_0|^2=4r^2$; multiply by $|\alpha|^2$: $1-\left(\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0\right)+|z_0|^2|\alpha|^2=4r^2|\alpha|^2$ ... (ii)

(ii) $-$ (i) removes the cross term: $\left(1-|\alpha|^2\right)+|z_0|^2\left(|\alpha|^2-1\right)=r^2\left(4|\alpha|^2-1\right)$, i.e. $\left(|\alpha|^2-1\right)\left(|z_0|^2-1\right)=r^2\left(4|\alpha|^2-1\right)$.
Use $|z_0|^2-1=\frac{r^2+2}{2}-1=\frac{r^2}{2}$: $\left(|\alpha|^2-1\right)\frac{r^2}{2}=r^2\left(4|\alpha|^2-1\right)$.
Cancel $r^2$: $|\alpha|^2-1=8|\alpha|^2-2\Rightarrow7|\alpha|^2=1\Rightarrow|\alpha|=\frac{1}{\sqrt7}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $|1-\bar a b|^2-|a-b|^2=\left(1-|a|^2\right)\left(1-|b|^2\right)$ to link the two circle conditions directly.
solution: Write $\frac1{\bar\alpha}-z_0=\frac{1-\bar\alpha z_0}{\bar\alpha}$, so $\left|\frac1{\bar\alpha}-z_0\right|^2=\frac{|1-\bar\alpha z_0|^2}{|\alpha|^2}=4r^2$, i.e. $|1-\bar\alpha z_0|^2=4r^2|\alpha|^2$.
Also $|\alpha-z_0|^2=r^2$.
The identity $|1-\bar\alpha z_0|^2-|\alpha-z_0|^2=1+|\alpha|^2|z_0|^2-|\alpha|^2-|z_0|^2=\left(1-|\alpha|^2\right)\left(1-|z_0|^2\right)$ is verified by expanding.
So $4r^2|\alpha|^2-r^2=\left(1-|\alpha|^2\right)\left(1-|z_0|^2\right)=\left(1-|\alpha|^2\right)\left(-\frac{r^2}{2}\right)$.
Dividing by $r^2$: $4|\alpha|^2-1=-\frac{1-|\alpha|^2}{2}\Rightarrow8|\alpha|^2-2=|\alpha|^2-1\Rightarrow|\alpha|^2=\frac17$, so $|\alpha|=\frac1{\sqrt7}$.

useful_results: For all complex $a,b$: $|1-\bar ab|^2-|a-b|^2=\left(1-|a|^2\right)\left(1-|b|^2\right)$ (the unit-disc identity behind Blaschke factors); it is positive for $a,b$ both inside or both outside the unit disc.
$\frac1{\bar\alpha}$ is the inversion of $\alpha$ in the unit circle: same direction from $O$, modulus $\frac1{|\alpha|}$.
To eliminate cross terms like $\alpha\bar z_0+\bar\alpha z_0$ between two circle equations, subtract them after matching the $|\alpha|$-factor (radical-axis idea).

concepts: Roots of unity: pairing, product and sum of roots
questions.question:
Let $z_k=\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi}{10}\right)+i\sin\left(\frac{2k\pi}{10}\right);\ k=1,2,\dots,9$. [JEE-Adv.2014]

Column-I
P. For each $z_k$ there exists a $z_j$ such that $z_k\cdot z_j=1$
Q. There exists a $k\in\{1,2,\dots,9\}$ such that $z_1\cdot z=z_k$ has no solution $z$ in the set of complex numbers.
R. $\frac{|1-z_1||1-z_2|\cdots|1-z_9|}{10}$ equals
S. $1-\sum_{k=1}^{9}\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi}{10}\right)$ equals

Column-II
1. True
2. False
3. $1$
4. $2$
questions.key_idea: $z_k$ are the tenth roots of unity other than 1: pair $z_k$ with $z_{10-k}$, and evaluate at $z=1$ the factorisation $\frac{z^{10}-1}{z-1}=\prod(z-z_k)$.
solution: (P) $z_kz_j=1$ gives $z_j=z_{10-k}$, because $z_kz_{10-k}=e^{i2\pi}=1$. Hence for each $k\in\{1,\dots,9\}$ there is such a $z_j$: True $\to$ (1).
(Q) $z_1\cdot z=z_k$ gives $z=z_{k-1}$ for $k=2,\dots,9$, and $z=1$ for $k=1$. A solution exists for every $k$, so the statement is False $\to$ (2).
(R) $z_1,\dots,z_9$ are the roots of $z^{10}=1$ other than $1$, so $\frac{z^{10}-1}{z-1}=1+z+\dots+z^9=(z-z_1)(z-z_2)\cdots(z-z_9)$.
(S) $\sum_{k=1}^9\cos\frac{2k\pi}{10}$ is the sum of the real parts of the roots of $z^{10}=1$ except $1$.
As $1+z_1+z_2+\dots+z_9=0$, we get $\sum\mathrm{Re}(z_k)+1=0$, so the sum is $-1$ and $1-(-1)=2\to$ (4).
So P-1, Q-2, R-3, S-4: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use trigonometry: pair $\theta$ with $\pi-\theta$ for the cosine sum, and evaluate the chord product $\prod2\sin\frac{k\pi}{10}$ with the exact values of $\sin18^\circ,\sin36^\circ,\dots$
solution: (S) Pair $k$ with $5-k$ for $k=1,\dots,4$: $\cos\frac{k\pi}{5}+\cos\frac{(5-k)\pi}{5}=\cos\theta+\cos(\pi-\theta)=0$.
Indices $6,\dots,9$ repeat the values of $4,\dots,1$ ($\cos\frac{2(10-k)\pi}{10}=\cos\frac{2k\pi}{10}$), and $k=5$ gives $\cos\pi=-1$.
(R) $|1-z_k|=2\sin\frac{k\pi}{10}$, so the product is $\prod_{k=1}^{9}2\sin\frac{k\pi}{10}=2^9\left(\sin18^\circ\sin54^\circ\sin36^\circ\sin72^\circ\right)^2\sin90^\circ$.
$\sin18^\circ\sin54^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt5+1}{4}=\frac14$ and $\sin36^\circ\sin72^\circ=\cos54^\circ\cos18^\circ=\frac12\left(\cos72^\circ+\cos36^\circ\right)=\frac{\sqrt5}{4}$.
Product $=512\cdot\left(\frac14\cdot\frac{\sqrt5}{4}\right)^2=512\cdot\frac{5}{256}=10$, so R $=1$: this agrees with the roots-of-unity result.

useful_results: For the $n$th roots of unity $1,z_1,\dots,z_{n-1}$: $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(x-z_k)=1+x+\dots+x^{n-1}$; at $x=1$, $\prod(1-z_k)=n$, so $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}2\sin\frac{k\pi}{n}=n$ (product of all chords from one vertex of a regular $n$-gon).
$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}z_k=0$ for $n\ge2$, hence $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2k\pi}{n}=-1$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\sin\frac{2k\pi}{n}=0$; check $n=3$: $\cos120^\circ+\cos240^\circ=-1$.
The inverse of a root of unity is its conjugate: $z_k^{-1}=\bar z_k=z_{n-k}$.

questions.question:
Match the following columns: [JEE-Adv.2015]

Column I
(A) In $\mathbb{R}^2$, if the magnitude of the projection vector of the vector $\alpha\hat i+\beta\hat j$ on $\sqrt3\hat i+\hat j$ is $\sqrt3$ and if $\alpha=2+\sqrt3\beta$, then possible value(s) of $|\alpha|$ is (are)
(B) Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers such that the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}-3ax^2-2,&x<1\\ bx+a^2,&x\ge1\end{cases}$ is differentiable for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Then possible value(s) of $a$ is (are)
(C) Let $\omega\neq1$ be a complex cube root of unity. If $\left(3-3\omega+2\omega^2\right)^{4n+3}+\left(2+3\omega-3\omega^2\right)^{4n+3}+\left(-3+2\omega+3\omega^2\right)^{4n+3}=0$, then possible value(s) of $n$ is (are)
(D) Let the harmonic mean of two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ be $4$. If $q$ is a positive real number such that $a,5,q,b$ is an arithmetic progression, then the value(s) of $|q-a|$ is (are)

Column II
(P) $1$   (Q) $2$   (R) $3$   (S) $4$   (T) $5$
questions.answer: (A)-P, Q; (B)-P, Q; (C)-P, Q, S, T; (D)-Q, T
questions.key_idea: In (C) the three bases are $a,\ a\omega,\ a\omega^2$, so the sum is $a^{4n+3}\left(1+\omega^{4n+3}+\omega^{2(4n+3)}\right)$, which vanishes unless $3\mid 4n+3$.
solution: (A) The projection of $\alpha\hat i+\beta\hat j$ on $\sqrt3\hat i+\hat j$ has magnitude $\left|(\alpha\hat i+\beta\hat j)\cdot\frac{\sqrt3\hat i+\hat j}{2}\right|=\sqrt3$, so $\sqrt3\alpha+\beta=\pm2\sqrt3$.
With $\beta=\frac{\alpha-2}{\sqrt3}$: $\sqrt3\alpha+\frac{\alpha-2}{\sqrt3}=\pm2\sqrt3\Rightarrow3\alpha+\alpha-2=\pm6\Rightarrow4\alpha=8$ or $-4$.
So $\alpha=2$ or $-1$, and $|\alpha|=2$ or $1$: (A) $\to$ P, Q.
(B) Continuity at $x=1$: $-3a-2=b+a^2$. Differentiability at $x=1$: $-6a=b$.
Substituting $b=-6a$: $-3a-2=-6a+a^2\Rightarrow a^2-3a+2=0\Rightarrow a=1,2$: (B) $\to$ P, Q.
(C) Let $a=3-3\omega+2\omega^2$. Then $a\omega=3\omega-3\omega^2+2\omega^3=2+3\omega-3\omega^2$ and $a\omega^2=3\omega^2-3+2\omega=-3+2\omega+3\omega^2$.
The sum is $a^{4n+3}\left[1+\omega^{4n+3}+\left(\omega^2\right)^{4n+3}\right]$, with $a=1-5\omega\neq0$.
The bracket is $0$ exactly when $\omega^{4n+3}\neq1$, i.e. $4n+3$ is not a multiple of 3, i.e. $n$ is not a multiple of 3. Among $1,2,3,4,5$ this gives $n=1,2,4,5$: (C) $\to$ P, Q, S, T.
(D) $\frac{2ab}{a+b}=4$ and $a,5,q,b$ in AP give $2q=5+b$ and $2\cdot5=a+q$, i.e. $q=10-a$ and $b=2q-5=15-2a$.
$2ab=4(a+b)\Rightarrow a(15-2a)=2a+2(15-2a)\Rightarrow2a^2-17a+30=0\Rightarrow a=6$ or $\frac52$.
Then $q=4$ or $\frac{15}{2}$ (both positive, with $b=3$ or $10$), so $|q-a|=2$ or $5$: (D) $\to$ Q, T.

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the AP by its common difference $d$ in (D) and substitute $\alpha=2+\sqrt3\beta$ directly in (A); both collapse to one-line equations.
solution: $|q-a|=|2d|=5$ or $2$ (valid: $d=\frac52$ gives $\frac52,5,\frac{15}{2},10$ and $d=-1$ gives $6,5,4,3$, all positive).
(A) Substitute $\alpha=2+\sqrt3\beta$ in $\sqrt3\alpha+\beta=\pm2\sqrt3$: $2\sqrt3+3\beta+\beta=\pm2\sqrt3$, so $4\beta=0$ or $-4\sqrt3$.
$\beta=0\Rightarrow\alpha=2$; $\beta=-\sqrt3\Rightarrow\alpha=-1$. So $|\alpha|=2$ or $1$, agreeing with the main solution.

useful_results: $z,\ z\omega,\ z\omega^2$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle centred at $0$: $\sum_{k=0}^{2}(z\omega^k)^m=z^m\left(1+\omega^m+\omega^{2m}\right)$, which is $3z^m$ if $3\mid m$ and $0$ otherwise. Recognise a rotation by $\omega$ between the terms.
A piecewise function is differentiable at the join iff the pieces agree in value and in derivative: two equations for two unknowns.
For an AP use the first term and common difference (or the middle term $m$ and $d$); it removes half the unknowns. $\mathrm{HM}(a,b)=\frac{2ab}{a+b}$ and $\mathrm{AM}\cdot\mathrm{HM}=\mathrm{GM}^2$.

questions.question: For any integer $k$, let $\alpha_k=\cos\left(\frac{k\pi}{7}\right)+i\sin\left(\frac{k\pi}{7}\right)$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. The value of the expression $\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{12}\left|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k\right|}{\sum_{k=1}^{3}\left|\alpha_{4k-1}-\alpha_{4k-2}\right|}$ is. [JEE-Adv.2015]
questions.key_idea: Consecutive $\alpha_k$ differ by the same rotation $e^{i\pi/7}$, so every term $|\alpha_{m+1}-\alpha_m|$ has the same value.
solution: $\alpha_k=\cos\frac{2k\pi}{14}+i\sin\frac{2k\pi}{14}=e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{14}}=e^{ik\pi/7}$.
$\left|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k\right|=\left|e^{i(k+1)\pi/7}-e^{ik\pi/7}\right|=\left|e^{ik\pi/7}\right|\left|e^{i\pi/7}-1\right|=\left|e^{i\pi/7}-1\right|$, the same for every $k$.
Numerator: $\sum_{k=1}^{12}\left|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k\right|=12\left|e^{i\pi/7}-1\right|$.
Denominator: $\left|\alpha_{4k-1}-\alpha_{4k-2}\right|=\left|e^{i(4k-1)\pi/7}-e^{i(4k-2)\pi/7}\right|=\left|e^{i\pi/7}-1\right|$ for each $k$, so the sum is $3\left|e^{i\pi/7}-1\right|$.
The ratio is $\frac{12\left|e^{i\pi/7}-1\right|}{3\left|e^{i\pi/7}-1\right|}=\frac{12}{3}=4$.
useful_results: $\left|e^{ia}-e^{ib}\right|=2\left|\sin\frac{a-b}{2}\right|$, so $|e^{i\theta}-1|=2\sin\frac\theta2$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$: chords of equal arc have equal length.
Points $e^{ik\theta}$ are the vertices of a regular polygon (or a spiral on the unit circle); every difference $\alpha_{k+m}-\alpha_k$ has modulus independent of $k$.
Instance: $|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|=2\sin\frac{\pi}{14}\approx0.445$ for all $k$, so only the number of terms matters.

questions.question: Let $z=\frac{-1+\sqrt3i}{2}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$ and $r,s\in\{1,2,3\}$. Let $P=\begin{pmatrix}(-z)^r&z^{2s}\\ z^{2s}&z^r\end{pmatrix}$ and $I$ be the identity matrix of order 2. Then the total number of ordered pairs $(r,s)$ for which $P^2=-I$ is. [JEE-Adv.2016]
questions.key_idea: Equating the off-diagonal entries of $P^2$ to $0$ forces $r$ odd, and the diagonal $-1$ becomes $1+\omega^s+\omega^{2r}=0$.
solution: $z=\omega$, a primitive cube root of unity, so $P=\begin{pmatrix}(-\omega)^r&\omega^{2s}\\ \omega^{2s}&\omega^r\end{pmatrix}$.
$P^2=\begin{pmatrix}(-\omega)^{2r}+\omega^{4s}&\omega^{2s}\left[(-\omega)^r+\omega^r\right]\\ \omega^{2s}\left[(-\omega)^r+\omega^r\right]&\omega^{4s}+\omega^{2r}\end{pmatrix}$.
$P^2=-I$ needs the off-diagonal entries $0$: $\omega^{2s}\omega^r\left[(-1)^r+1\right]=0\Rightarrow(-1)^r=-1\Rightarrow r$ is odd.
It needs the diagonal entries $-1$: $\omega^{2r}+\omega^{4s}=-1$, and since $\omega^{4s}=\omega^s$ this is $1+\omega^s+\omega^{2r}=0$.

$1+u+v=0$ with $u,v$ cube roots of unity holds only when $\{u,v\}=\{\omega,\omega^2\}$; so $3
mid s$, $3
mid 2r$ and $\omega^s
eq\omega^{2r}$.
$r$ odd and $r\in\{1,2,3\}$ gives $r=1$ or $3$; $r=3$ is rejected since $\omega^{6}=1$, leaving $r=1$ and $\omega^{2r}=\omega^2$.
Then $\omega^s=\omega$, so $s=1$ (as $s\in\{1,2,3\}$). Only $(r,s)=(1,1)$: the number of ordered pairs is $1$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes 'r != odd' (it must be 'r is odd', as the off-diagonal entry vanishes only for odd r) and jumps from 1+w^s+w^(2r)=0 to r=s=1 without the case check (r=3, s=2,3). Added.

alternate_solutions.idea: For odd $r$ the matrix has trace $0$, so by the Cayley-Hamilton theorem $P^2=-\det(P)\,I$ and the condition is $\det P=1$.
solution: If $r$ is even, $(-\omega)^r+\omega^r=2\omega^r\neq0$ makes the off-diagonal entries of $P^2$ non-zero, so $P^2\neq-I$. Hence $r$ is odd.
For odd $r$: $(-\omega)^r=-\omega^r$, so $P=\begin{pmatrix}-\omega^r&\omega^{2s}\\ \omega^{2s}&\omega^r\end{pmatrix}$ has trace $0$.
Cayley-Hamilton: $P^2-(\mathrm{tr}P)P+(\det P)I=0\Rightarrow P^2=-(\det P)\,I$. So $P^2=-I\iff\det P=1$.
$\det P=-\omega^{2r}-\omega^{4s}=1\iff\omega^{2r}+\omega^{4s}=-1$.
$r=3$: $1+\omega^{4s}=-1$ is impossible ($|\omega^{4s}|=1$ but $-2$ has modulus 2). $r=1$: $\omega^2+\omega^{4s}=-1=\omega+\omega^2\Rightarrow\omega^{s}=\omega\Rightarrow s=1$.
So the only pair is $(1,1)$: the answer is $1$.

useful_results: For a $2\times2$ matrix of trace $0$, $P^2=-\det(P)\,I$ (Cayley-Hamilton). So $P^2=\pm I$ reduces to $\det P=\mp1$ with no multiplication needed.
For cube roots of unity, $1+u+v=0$ iff $\{u,v\}=\{\omega,\omega^2\}$; and $\omega^m$ depends only on $m\bmod3$.
$(-\omega)^r=(-1)^r\omega^r$: separate the sign from the power before multiplying matrices.

questions.question: Let $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a^2+b^2\neq0$. Suppose $S=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:z=\frac{1}{a+ibt},\ t\in\mathbb{R},\ t\neq0\right\}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. If $z=x+iy$ and $z\in S$, then $(x,y)$ lies on [JEE-Adv.2016]
options: the circle with radius $\frac1{2a}$ and centre $\left(\frac1{2a},0\right)$ for $a>0,\ b\neq0$
the circle with radius $-\frac1{2a}$ and centre $\left(-\frac1{2a},0\right)$ for $a<0,\ b\neq0$
questions.key_idea: Rationalise $\frac1{a+ibt}$ to get $x,y$ in terms of $t$; then $x^2+y^2=\frac{x}{a}$ eliminates $t$.
solution: $x+iy=\frac{1}{a+ibt}=\frac{a-ibt}{a^2+b^2t^2}$, so $x=\frac{a}{a^2+b^2t^2}$ and $y=\frac{-bt}{a^2+b^2t^2}$.
(C) For $b=0$ (so $a\neq0$): $x=\frac1a,\ y=0$: the point lies on the $x$-axis. True.
(D) For $a=0$ (so $b\neq0$): $x=0,\ y=\frac{-1}{bt}$: the point lies on the $y$-axis. True.
For $a\neq0,\ b\neq0$: $x^2+y^2=\frac{a^2+b^2t^2}{\left(a^2+b^2t^2\right)^2}=\frac{1}{a^2+b^2t^2}=\frac{x}{a}$, so $x^2+y^2-\frac{x}{a}=0$.
This is the circle with centre $\left(\frac{1}{2a},0\right)$ and radius $\left|\frac1{2a}\right|$.
(A) For $a>0$ the radius is $\frac1{2a}$ and the centre is $\left(\frac1{2a},0\right)$: True.
(B) For $a<0$ the centre is $\left(\frac{1}{2a},0\right)$ (negative), not $\left(-\frac1{2a},0\right)$ as stated: False.
questions.correction_note: PDF gives only the parametric form and the circle x^2+y^2-x/a=0 and does not examine option (B) at all. Verdict on (B) added: for a<0 the centre is (1/(2a),0), not (-1/(2a),0). Key ACD unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $z=\frac1w$ with $w=a+ibt$ on a vertical line: inversion maps a line not through $0$ to a circle through $0$, a line through $0$ to a line through $0$.
solution: $z=\frac1w$ where $w=a+ibt$; as $t$ varies, $w$ describes the line $\mathrm{Re}\,w=a$ (if $b\neq0$), minus the point $w=a$ ($t=0$), and just the point $a$ if $b=0$.

If $a\neq0,\ b\neq0$: the line $\mathrm{Re}\,w=a$ does not pass through $0$; its inverse is a circle through $0$ with centre on the real axis. The point of the line nearest to $0$ is $w=a$, which maps to $z=\frac1a$, the far end of a diameter.
So the circle has diameter from $0$ to $\frac1a$: centre $\frac1{2a}$, radius $\left|\frac{1}{2a}\right|$. For $a>0$ this is (A); for $a<0$ the centre $\frac1{2a}$ is negative, so (B) is false.
If $b=0,\ a\neq0$: $z=\frac1a$, a point on the real axis: (C).
If $a=0,\ b\neq0$: $w=ibt$ is the imaginary axis through $0$; $z=\frac{-i}{bt}$ is again on the imaginary axis: (D). So (A), (C), (D).

useful_results: Inversion $w\mapsto\frac1w$: a line not through $0$ at distance $d$ becomes a circle through $0$ of diameter $\frac1d$ (centre on the perpendicular from $0$); a line through $0$ stays a line through $0$.
Quick locus check: $\left|z-\frac1{2a}\right|^2=\frac1{4a^2}\iff x^2+y^2=\frac xa$; verify with $t=1$: $z=\frac{1}{a+ib}$ gives $|z|^2=\frac1{a^2+b^2}=\frac{\mathrm{Re}\,z}{a}$.
To eliminate a real parameter from $x(t),y(t)$ look for a combination such as $x^2+y^2$ that is a simple function of $x$ or $y$.

questions.question: Let $a,b,x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that $a-b=1$ and $y\neq0$. If the complex number $z=x+iy$ satisfies $\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac{az+b}{z+1}\right)=y$, then which of the following is(are) possible value(s) of $x$? [JEE-Adv.2017]
questions.key_idea: The imaginary part collapses to $\frac{(a-b)\,y}{|z+1|^2}$, so with $a-b=1$ and $y\neq0$ the condition is $|z+1|^2=1$.
solution: $\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac{a(x+iy)+b}{x+iy+1}\right)=y$.
Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: $\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac{\left[(ax+b)+iay\right]\left[(x+1)-iy\right]}{(x+1)^2+y^2}\right)=y$.
The imaginary part of the numerator is $ay(x+1)-y(ax+b)=y(a-b)$, so $\frac{ay(x+1)-y(ax+b)}{(x+1)^2+y^2}=y$.
Since $y\neq0$, cancel $y$: $a-b=(x+1)^2+y^2$.
$x+1=\pm\sqrt{1-y^2}$, i.e. $x=-1\pm\sqrt{1-y^2}$ (real only for $0<|y|\le1$).
So the possible values are $-1+\sqrt{1-y^2}$ and $-1-\sqrt{1-y^2}$: options (B) and (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide first: $\frac{az+b}{z+1}=a-\frac{a-b}{z+1}=a-\frac1{z+1}$, and $\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac1w\right)=-\frac{\mathrm{Im}\,w}{|w|^2}$.
solution: $a$ is real, so $\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac{az+b}{z+1}\right)=-\mathrm{Im}\left(\frac{1}{z+1}\right)$.
For $w=z+1=(x+1)+iy$: $\mathrm{Im}\frac1w=\frac{-y}{|w|^2}$, so the condition becomes $\frac{y}{(x+1)^2+y^2}=y$.
As $y\neq0$: $(x+1)^2+y^2=1$, i.e. $z$ lies on the circle of centre $-1$ and radius $1$.
Hence $x=-1\pm\sqrt{1-y^2}$: options (B), (D).

useful_results: $\frac{az+b}{cz+d}=\frac ac-\frac{ad-bc}{c(cz+d)}$: divide a Möbius expression into a constant plus $\frac{k}{\text{linear}}$ before taking real or imaginary parts.
$\mathrm{Im}\frac1w=-\frac{\mathrm{Im}\,w}{|w|^2}$ and $\mathrm{Re}\frac1w=\frac{\mathrm{Re}\,w}{|w|^2}$.
Always keep the domain: $x=-1\pm\sqrt{1-y^2}$ needs $|y|\le1$, so options with $\sqrt{1+y^2}$ can never be values of $x$ here.

questions.question: For a non-zero complex number $z$ let $\arg(z)$ denote the principal argument with $-\pi<\arg(z)\le\pi$. Then, which of the following statement(s) is (are) FALSE? [JEE-Adv.2018]
options: The function $f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\pi,\pi]$ defined by $f(t)=\arg(-1+it)$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, is continuous at all points of $\mathbb{R}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$
For any two non-zero complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$, $\arg\left(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\right)-\arg(z_1)+\arg(z_2)$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$

For any three given distinct complex numbers $z_1,z_2$ and $z_3$, the locus of the point $z$ satisfying the condition $\arg\left(\frac{(z-z_1)(z_2-z_3)}{(z-z_3)(z_2-z_1)}\right)=\pi$ lies on a straight line
questions.key_idea: $\arg$ has a jump of $2\pi$ across the negative real axis, and a real-negative cross-ratio describes a circle through $z_1,z_2,z_3$, not a line.
solution: (A) $-1-i$ is in the third quadrant at $225^\circ$, so $\arg(-1-i)=-\frac{3\pi}{4}\neq\frac\pi4$. Statement (A) is false.
(B) $f(t)=\arg(-1+it)=\pi-\tan^{-1}t$ for $t\ge0$ and $-\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}t\right)$ for $t<0$.
$f(0)=\pi$ and $\lim_{t\to0^+}f(t)=\pi$ but $\lim_{t\to0^-}f(t)=-\pi$. So $f$ is discontinuous at $t=0$: (B) is false.
(C) $\arg\left(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\right)=\arg z_1-\arg z_2+2n\pi$ for some integer $n$ (the principal value is brought back to $(-\pi,\pi]$).
So $\arg\left(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\right)-\arg z_1+\arg z_2=2n\pi$: (C) is true.

(D) $\arg\frac{(z-z_1)(z_2-z_3)}{(z-z_3)(z_2-z_1)}=\pi$ says the cross-ratio of $z,z_1,z_2,z_3$ is a negative real number, so $z$ lies on the circle through $z_1,z_2,z_3$ (the arc opposite $z_2$ over the chord $z_1z_3$).
For non-collinear $z_1,z_2,z_3$ this is an arc of a circle, not a straight line: (D) is false.
The false statements are (A), (B), (D).
questions.correction_note: PDF (C) writes 'Arg(z1/z) = Arg z1 + Arg z2 + 2n pi' (typo: it should read Arg(z1/z2) = Arg z1 - Arg z2 + 2n pi, otherwise the final expression is not 2n pi); (D) says only 'If is circle' (text lost). Both rewritten; key ABD unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Geometric view: $\arg$ jumps by $2\pi$ at the branch cut $(-\infty,0)$, and the cross-ratio map $z\mapsto\frac{(z-z_1)(z_2-z_3)}{(z-z_3)(z_2-z_1)}$ is a Möbius map.
solution: (B) The point $-1+it$ moves up the vertical line $\mathrm{Re}=-1$; at $t=0$ it crosses the negative real axis (the branch cut of $\arg$), from below ($\arg\to-\pi$) to above ($\arg\to\pi$). So $f$ jumps by $2\pi$ at $t=0$: not continuous.
(D) $M(z)=\frac{(z-z_1)(z_2-z_3)}{(z-z_3)(z_2-z_1)}$ is a Möbius map with $M(z_1)=0,\ M(z_2)=1,\ M(z_3)=\infty$.
Möbius maps send lines and circles to lines and circles; the real axis passes through $0,1,\infty$, so its pre-image is the circle (or line, if collinear) through $z_1,z_2,z_3$.
The condition $\arg M(z)=\pi$ picks the negative real axis, i.e. the part of that circle not containing $z_2$ (where $M<0$): an arc of a circle for non-collinear $z_1,z_2,z_3$, not a line.
So (B) and (D) are false; (A) is false by direct computation, giving (A, B, D).

useful_results: $\arg(z_1z_2)\equiv\arg z_1+\arg z_2$ and $\arg\frac{z_1}{z_2}\equiv\arg z_1-\arg z_2\pmod{2\pi}$: the principal values may differ by a multiple of $2\pi$, never by anything else.
The principal argument is discontinuous exactly on the negative real axis (jump $2\pi$): the function $t\mapsto\arg(-1+it)$ jumps at $t=0$.

Cross-ratio: $\arg\frac{(z-z_1)(z_2-z_3)}{(z-z_3)(z_2-z_1)}$ is a constant $\iff z$ lies on a circle arc through $z_1,z_3$; constant $0$ or $\pi$ means the whole circle through $z_1,z_2,z_3$ (or the line if they are collinear).
Beware 'for any three given' statements: a locus claimed to be a line is false unless the points are collinear.

questions.question: Let $s,t,r$ be non-zero complex numbers and $L$ be the set of solutions $z=x+iy$ ($x,y\in\mathbb{R},\ i=\sqrt{-1}$) of the equation $sz+t\bar z+r=0$, where $\bar z=x-iy$. Then, which of the following statement(s) is (are) TRUE? [JEE-Adv.2018]
options: If $L$ has exactly one element, then $|s|\neq|t|$
If $|s|=|t|$, then $L$ has infinitely many elements
The number of elements in $L\cap\{z:|z-1+i|=5\}$ is at most $2$
If $L$ has more than one element, then $L$ has infinitely many elements
questions.key_idea: $sz+t\bar z+r=0$ and its conjugate form a linear system in $(z,\bar z)$ with determinant $|s|^2-|t|^2$: unique solution iff $|s|\neq|t|$.
solution: $sz+t\bar z+r=0$ ... (1). Taking the conjugate: $\bar s\bar z+\bar tz+\bar r=0$ ... (2).
(1)+(2): $\left(t+\bar s\right)\bar z+\left(s+\bar t\right)z+\left(r+\bar r\right)=0$. (1)$-$(2): $\left(t-\bar s\right)\bar z+\left(s-\bar t\right)z+\left(r-\bar r\right)=0$.
These two equations are the two real linear equations in $x,y$ (real and imaginary parts of (1)).

Unique solution requires the coefficient ratios to differ: $ rac{t+ ar s}{t- ar s}
eq rac{s+ ar t}{s- ar t}$; simplifying gives $|t|
eq|s|$. So if $L$ has exactly one element, $|s|
eq|t|$: (A) is true.
Cross-multiplying, $(t+\bar s)(s-\bar t)-(s+\bar t)(t-\bar s)=2\left(|s|^2-|t|^2\right)$, so the two lines have equal slopes (are parallel or coincide) exactly when $|s|=|t|$.
If $|s|=|t|$ the lines are parallel: they either coincide (infinitely many solutions) or do not meet (no solution). So $L$ can be empty and (B) is false.
(C) If $L$ is a line (or a single point or empty), its intersection with the circle $|z-1+i|=5$ has at most $2$ points: (C) is true.
(D) If $L$ has more than one element then the two lines coincide, so $L$ is a whole line with infinitely many elements: (D) is true.

alternate_solutions.idea: View $z\mapsto sz+t\bar z$ as a real-linear map of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with determinant $|s|^2-|t|^2$: solutions of $T(z)=-r$ form either a point, a line, or nothing.
solution: $T(z)=sz+t\bar z$ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear on $\mathbb{R}^2\cong\mathbb{C}$. Multiplication by $s$ has determinant $|s|^2$; $z\mapsto\bar z$ has determinant $-1$, and $z\mapsto t\bar z$ has determinant $-|t|^2$.
The determinant of $T$ is $|s|^2-|t|^2$ (checked on $s=1,t=1$: $T(x+iy)=2x$, det $0$; on $s=2,t=1$: $T(z)=2z+\bar z=3x+iy$, det $3=4-1$).
If $\det T\neq0$, $T$ is invertible and $T(z)=-r$ has exactly one solution. So exactly one element forces $|s|\neq|t|$: (A).
If $\det T=0$ (and $s,t\neq0$), $T$ has rank $1$: $T(z)=-r$ has either no solution or a whole line (a translate of the kernel line). So $|s|=|t|$ need not give infinitely many: (B) false.
In every case $L$ is empty, a point or a line, so it meets a circle in at most $2$ points: (C). More than one solution means the line case, hence infinitely many: (D).

useful_results: $sz+t\bar z=c$ ($s,t\neq0$) has a unique solution iff $|s|\neq|t|$, namely $z=\frac{\bar sc-t\bar c}{|s|^2-|t|^2}$; for $|s|=|t|$ it is a line or empty.
A single equation in $z,\bar z$ that is linear represents a line (e.g. $\bar az+a\bar z+b=0$ with $b$ real is a line), the intersection of such a line with a circle has at most two points.
The $\mathbb{R}$-linear map $z\mapsto sz+t\bar z$ has determinant $|s|^2-|t|^2$ (rotation-scaling minus reflection-scaling parts).

questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all complex numbers $z$ satisfying $|z-2+i|\ge\sqrt5$. If the complex number $z_0$ is such that $\frac{1}{|z_0-1|}$ is the maximum of the set $\left\{\frac1{|z-1|}:z\in S\right\}$, then the principal argument of $\frac{4-z_0-\bar z_0}{z_0-\bar z_0+2i}$ is: [JEE-Adv.2019]
questions.key_idea: Maximising $\frac1{|z-1|}$ means minimising the distance from $1$; since $1$ lies inside the circle, the nearest point of $S$ is on the circle along the ray from the centre through $1$.
solution: $\frac{1}{|z-1|}$ is maximum when $|z-1|$ is minimum: $z_0$ is the point of $S$ nearest to $1$.
$S$ is the exterior (with boundary) of the circle with centre $C=(2,-1)$ and radius $\sqrt5$. The distance $|1-C|=\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt2<\sqrt5$, so the point $1$ lies inside the circle.
The nearest point of the exterior to an interior point is the point where the ray from the centre $C$ through $1$ meets the circle: $z_0=C+\sqrt5\cdot\frac{1-C}{|1-C|}$.
$1-C=-1+i$ and $|1-C|=\sqrt2$, so $z_0=(2-i)+\sqrt{\tfrac52}(-1+i)$, giving $x_0=2-\sqrt{\tfrac52}$ and $y_0=-1+\sqrt{\tfrac52}$.
$4-z_0-\bar z_0=4-2x_0=2\sqrt{\tfrac52}=\sqrt{10}$, a positive real number.
$z_0-\bar z_0+2i=2iy_0+2i=2i(y_0+1)=2i\sqrt{\tfrac52}=i\sqrt{10}$.
The ratio is $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{i\sqrt{10}}=\frac1i=-i$, whose principal argument is $-\frac\pi2$: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $z_0$ by the triangle inequality $|z-1|\ge|z-C|-|C-1|\ge\sqrt5-\sqrt2$, then use that $z_0-C$ is a positive multiple of $-1+i$ to evaluate the expression without coordinates.
solution: For $z\in S$: $|z-1|\ge|z-C|-|1-C|\ge\sqrt5-\sqrt2$, with equality only if $|z-C|=\sqrt5$ and $z-C$ is in the same direction as $1-C=-1+i$.
So $z_0-C=\lambda(-1+i)$ with $\lambda>0$ (and $\lambda\sqrt2=\sqrt5$).
Then $x_0=2-\lambda$ and $y_0=-1+\lambda$, so $2-x_0=\lambda=y_0+1$.
$\frac{4-z_0-\bar z_0}{z_0-\bar z_0+2i}=\frac{2(2-x_0)}{2i(y_0+1)}=\frac{2\lambda}{2i\lambda}=-i$.
Hence the principal argument is $-\frac\pi2$ (option B), independent of the actual value of $\lambda$.

useful_results: Nearest point of the exterior of a circle to an interior point $P$: the point where the ray from the centre through $P$ meets the circle (distance $r-|PC|$); farthest point of the disc from $P$ is on the opposite ray.

For $z=x+iy$: $z+\bar z=2x$ and $z-\bar z=2iy$, so $\frac{\text{real}}{\text{imaginary}\cdot i}$-type expressions are purely imaginary: their argument is $\pm\frac\pi2$ and the sign comes from the sign of the real ratio.
Triangle inequality $|z-P|\ge|z-C|-|C-P|$ gives distance bounds with equality when $z-C$ is parallel to $P-C$.

concepts: Cube roots of unity: modulus of $a+b\omega+c\omega^2$

questions.question: Let $\omega\neq1$ be a cube root of unity. Then the minimum of the set $\left\{|a+b\omega+c\omega^2|^2:\ a,b,c\ \text{distinct non-zero integers}\right\}$ equals ____ [JEE-Adv.2019]
questions.key_idea: $|a+b\omega+c\omega^2|^2=\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]$, so it is the spread of three distinct integers.
solution: $|a+b\omega+c\omega^2|^2=\left(a+b\omega+c\omega^2\right)\left(a+b\omega^2+c\omega\right)$ (conjugate of $\omega$ is $\omega^2$).
Expanding with $\omega^3=1$ and $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$: $=a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca$.
$=\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]$.
For distinct integers every difference is a non-zero integer. If $a<b<c$ then $(a-b)^2\ge1$, $(b-c)^2\ge1$ and $(c-a)^2=\left((c-b)+(b-a)\right)^2\ge4$, so the value is at least $\frac12(1+1+4)=3$.
Equality holds for three consecutive non-zero integers: $a=1,b=2,c=3$ gives $\frac12(1+1+4)=3$.
So the minimum is $3$.
questions.correction_note: PDF puts a=1, b=2, c=3 and states 'minimum = 3' without showing that nothing smaller is possible. The bound (c-a)^2 >= 4 for distinct integers (the largest gap is at least 2) was added. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Shift by $c$: since $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$, $a+b\omega+c\omega^2=(a-c)+(b-c)\omega$, and $|u+v\omega|^2=u^2-uv+v^2$ is the Eisenstein norm.
solution: $a+b\omega+c\omega^2=(a-c)+(b-c)\omega$ because $\omega^2=-1-\omega$. Put $u=a-c,\ v=b-c$: distinct non-zero $a,b,c$ means $u,v\neq0$ and $u\neq v$.
$|u+v\omega|^2=u^2-uv+v^2=\left(u-\frac v2\right)^2+\frac{3v^2}{4}$.
If $|v|\ge2$ then this is $\ge3$. If $|v|=1$, take $v=1$: $u^2-u+1$ with $u\neq0,1$ is $\ge3$ (at $u=-1$ or $2$); $v=-1$ is symmetric.
The value $3$ is attained at $(u,v)=(-1,1)$, i.e. $a=c-1,\ b=c+1$: for example $c=2$: $(a,b,c)=(1,3,2)$.
So the minimum is $3$, in agreement with the main solution.

useful_results: $|a+b\omega+c\omega^2|^2=a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca=\frac12\sum(a-b)^2$ for real $a,b,c$; it is $0$ iff $a=b=c$.
It depends only on differences (adding the same number to $a,b,c$ adds $k(1+\omega+\omega^2)=0$); three distinct integers have gaps $\ge1,1$ and total $\ge2$.
Eisenstein integers: $|u+v\omega|^2=u^2-uv+v^2$ takes the values $0,1,3,4,7,\dots$ and never $2$ or $5$ (check $u,v\in\{0,\pm1,\pm2\}$).

questions.key_idea: Completing the square, $z^2+z+1=\left(z+\frac12\right)^2+\frac34$; $|w^2+\frac34|=1$ bounds $|w|$ between $\frac12$ and $\frac{\sqrt7}{2}$.

$\left|z+\frac12\right|=\frac12\left[(4\cos\theta-3)^2+(4\sin\theta)^2\right]^{1/4}=\frac12(25-24\cos\theta)^{1/4}$.
As $\cos\theta$ varies in $[-1,1]$, $25-24\cos\theta\in[1,49]$, so $\left|z+\frac12\right|\in\left[\frac12,\frac{\sqrt7}{2}\right]$.
So $\left|z+\frac12\right|\ge\frac12$ always: (C) is true. The upper end $\frac{\sqrt7}{2}>\frac12$ is attained, so $\left|z+\frac12\right|\le\frac12$ fails for some $z\in S$: (A) is false.
$|2z|=\left|(2z+1)-1\right|\le|2z+1|+1\le\sqrt7+1$ (triangle inequality), so $|z|\le\frac{1+\sqrt7}{2}\approx1.82\le2$: (B) is true.
As $\theta$ varies continuously over $[0,2\pi)$ it gives infinitely many different values of $z$, so $S$ is infinite, not four points: (D) is false.
questions.correction_note: PDF does not state why (A) and (D) fail (it only shows the range [1/2, sqrt7/2] and |z|<=2). Verdicts for (A) and (D) were added; the working of (B) and (C) is the PDF's.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $w=z+\frac12$: the condition is $\left|w^2+\frac34\right|=1$, and the triangle inequality bounds $|w|^2$ directly.
solution: $z^2+z+1=\left(z+\frac12\right)^2+\frac34=w^2+\frac34$ with $w=z+\frac12$, so $S$ is $\left|w^2+\frac34\right|=1$.
$|w^2|=\left|\left(w^2+\frac34\right)-\frac34\right|\ge1-\frac34=\frac14$, so $|w|\ge\frac12$: (C) is true.
$|w^2|\le\left|w^2+\frac34\right|+\frac34=\frac74$, so $|w|\le\frac{\sqrt7}{2}$, and then $|z|\le|w|+\frac12\le\frac{1+\sqrt7}{2}<2$: (B) is true.
(A) fails: $w^2=-\frac74$ satisfies $\left|-\frac74+\frac34\right|=1$, giving $|w|=\frac{\sqrt7}{2}>\frac12$ (i.e. $z=-\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt7}{2}i$).
(D) fails: $\left|w^2+\frac34\right|=1$ is a closed curve (a Cassini-type oval), containing infinitely many points. So (B), (C).

A locus given by one real equation in the plane ($|f(z)|=1$) is a curve, normally an infinite set; do not count roots unless it is $f(z)=$ constant.

questions.question: For a complex number $z$, let $\mathrm{Re}(z)$ denote the real part of $z$. Let $S$ be the set of all complex numbers $z$ satisfying $z^4-|z|^4=4iz^2$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Then the minimum possible value of $|z_1-z_2|^2$, where $z_1,z_2\in S$ with $\mathrm{Re}(z_1)>0$ and $\mathrm{Re}(z_2)<0$, is ____ [JEE-(Adv)2020]
questions.key_idea: For $z\neq0$ the equation reduces to $z^2-\bar z^2=4i$, i.e. $xy=1$: the problem is the distance between the two branches of a rectangular hyperbola.
solution: $z^4-|z|^4=4iz^2$ with $|z|^4=z^2\bar z^2$. Since $\mathrm{Re}\,z\neq0$ we have $z\neq0$; divide by $z^2$: $z^2-\bar z^2=4i$.
Put $z=x+iy$: $z+\bar z=2x$ and $z-\bar z=2iy$, so (1) becomes $4ixy=4i$, i.e. $xy=1$.
$S\setminus\{0\}$ is the rectangular hyperbola $xy=1$, with branches in the first and third quadrants.
$z_1$ (with $\mathrm{Re}>0$) lies on the first-quadrant branch and $z_2$ (with $\mathrm{Re}<0$) on the third-quadrant branch.
The minimum distance between the two branches is the length of the transverse axis, between the vertices $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$: $|z_1-z_2|_{\min}=2\sqrt2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take $z_1=\left(p,\frac1p\right)$, $z_2=\left(-q,-\frac1q\right)$ and bound the squared distance by AM-GM.
solution: On $xy=1$ with $x>0$: $z_1=p+\frac ip$, and with $x<0$: $z_2=-q-\frac iq$, where $p,q>0$.
By AM-GM, $(p+q)^2\ge4pq$, so $|z_1-z_2|^2\ge4pq+\frac{4pq}{p^2q^2}=4\left(pq+\frac{1}{pq}\right)$.
$pq+\frac1{pq}\ge2$, so $|z_1-z_2|^2\ge8$, with equality when $p=q$ and $pq=1$, i.e. $p=q=1$.
So the minimum of $|z_1-z_2|^2$ is $8$.

useful_results: $z^2-\bar z^2=4ixy$ and $z^2+\bar z^2=2(x^2-y^2)$: so $\mathrm{Im}(z^2)=2xy$ and $\mathrm{Re}(z^2)=x^2-y^2$. $\mathrm{Im}(z^2)=c$ is the rectangular hyperbola $xy=\frac c2$.
For $xy=k^2$ the two vertices are $\pm(k,k)$ and the minimum distance between branches is $2\sqrt2\,k$ (here $k=1$: $2\sqrt2$).
Dividing an equation by $z^2$ is legal only when $z=0$ is excluded: check $z=0$ separately (here $\mathrm{Re}\,z\neq0$ excludes it).

questions.question: For any complex number $w=c+id$, let $\arg(w)\in(-\pi,\pi]$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be real numbers such that for all complex numbers $z=x+iy$ satisfying $\arg\left(\frac{z+\alpha}{z+\beta}\right)=\frac\pi4$, the ordered pair $(x,y)$ lies on the circle $x^2+y^2+5x-3y+4=0$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE? [JEE-(Adv)2021]
questions.key_idea: $\arg(z+\alpha)-\arg(z+\beta)=\frac\pi4$ becomes $\tan^{-1}$-difference $=\frac\pi4$, giving the circle $x^2+y^2+(\alpha+\beta)x+(\alpha-\beta)y+\alpha\beta=0$ to compare with the given one.
solution: $\arg\left(\frac{z+\alpha}{z+\beta}\right)=\frac\pi4\Rightarrow\arg(z+\alpha)-\arg(z+\beta)=\frac\pi4$ (the real numbers $\alpha,\beta$ keep both points on the real axis).
$\arg(x+\alpha+iy)-\arg(x+\beta+iy)=\frac\pi4\Rightarrow\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{\alpha+x}-\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{\beta+x}=\frac\pi4$.
Taking $\tan$: $\frac{\frac{y}{\alpha+x}-\frac{y}{\beta+x}}{1+\frac{y}{\alpha+x}\cdot\frac{y}{\beta+x}}=\tan\frac\pi4=1$.
Numerator $\times(\alpha+x)(\beta+x)$: $\frac{y(\beta+x)-y(\alpha+x)}{(\alpha+x)(\beta+x)+y^2}=1\Rightarrow\beta y-\alpha y=\alpha\beta+x(\alpha+\beta)+x^2+y^2$.
So the locus is $x^2+y^2+x(\alpha+\beta)+y(\alpha-\beta)+\alpha\beta=0$.
Compare with $x^2+y^2+5x-3y+4=0$: $\alpha+\beta=5$, $\alpha-\beta=-3$ and $\alpha\beta=4$.
The first two give $\alpha=1,\ \beta=4$, and indeed $\alpha\beta=4$. So (B) $\alpha\beta=4$ and (D) $\beta=4$ are true; (A) and (C) are false.

alternate_solutions.idea: Inscribed-angle view: a constant angle $\frac\pi4$ subtended by the chord joining $(-\alpha,0)$ and $(-\beta,0)$ gives a circle through those two points, which are found from $y=0$ in the given circle.
solution: $\arg\frac{z+\alpha}{z+\beta}$ is the angle at $z$ between the points $-\beta$ and $-\alpha$ on the real axis; constant angle means $z$ moves on a circular arc through $(-\alpha,0)$ and $(-\beta,0)$.
The given circle meets $y=0$ where $x^2+5x+4=0$, i.e. at $x=-1$ and $x=-4$. So $\{-\alpha,-\beta\}=\{-1,-4\}$ and $\alpha\beta=4$: (B) is true.

Orientation: the circle has centre $\left(-\frac52,\frac32\right)$ above the axis, so $z$ is on the upper arc. For $z$ above the axis, a point further to the right sees $z$ at a larger direction angle, so $\arg(z+\alpha)>\arg(z+\beta)$ means $-\alpha>-\beta$, i.e. $-\alpha=-1,\ -\beta=-4$.
So $\alpha=1,\ \beta=4$ and $\frac\pi4$ matches the inscribed angle: the chord has length $3$, radius $R=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}$ gives $2R\sin\frac\pi4=3$.
Hence $\beta=4$ (D) and $\alpha\beta=4$ (B) are true.

useful_results: $\arg\frac{z-a}{z-b}=\theta$ (constant, $0<\theta<\pi$) is an arc of a circle through $a$ and $b$; $\theta=\pi$ is the segment between $a$ and $b$, $\theta=0$ the rest of the line.
For the circle through $(p,0),(q,0)$ the equation is $x^2+y^2-(p+q)x+ky+pq=0$: the sum of the intercepts is $-(\text{coefficient of }x)$ and the product is the constant term.
With $\arg\frac{z+\alpha}{z+\beta}=\frac\pi4$ the locus is $x^2+y^2+(\alpha+\beta)x+(\alpha-\beta)y+\alpha\beta=0$.

solution: Dividing the fraction by $z$: $w=1+\frac{6}{2\left(2z+\frac1z\right)-3}$.

questions.question: Let $\bar z$ denote the complex conjugate of a complex number $z$ and let $i=\sqrt{-1}$. In the set of complex numbers, the number of distinct roots of the equation $\bar z-z^2=i\left(\bar z+z^2\right)$ is ____ [JEE-(Adv)2022]
questions.key_idea: Collect $\bar z$ and $z^2$ to get $z^2=-i\bar z$, then split into real and imaginary parts.
solution: $\bar z-z^2=i\bar z+iz^2\Rightarrow(1-i)\bar z=(1+i)z^2$.
$z^2=\frac{1-i}{1+i}\bar z=\frac{-2i}{2}\bar z=-i\bar z$.
Let $z=x+iy$: $(x^2-y^2)+i(2xy)=-i(x-iy)=-y-ix$.
Real parts: $x^2-y^2+y=0$ ... (1). Imaginary parts: $2xy=-x$, i.e. $(2y+1)x=0$ ... (2).
Case I, $x=0$: (1) gives $y(1-y)=0$, so $y=0$ or $1$: the points $(0,0)$ and $(0,1)$, i.e. $z=0,\ i$.
Case II, $y=-\frac12$: (1) gives $x^2-\frac14-\frac12=0$, so $x=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$: the points $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)$ and $\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)$.
These four points are distinct: the number of distinct roots is $4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Polar form: $z^2=-i\bar z$ gives $r^2e^{2i\theta}=re^{-i(\pi/2+\theta)}$, so $r=0$ or $r=1$ with $e^{3i\theta}=-i$: three unit roots plus $z=0$.
solution: From $z^2=-i\bar z$, take $z=re^{i\theta}$: $r^2e^{2i\theta}=e^{-i\pi/2}\,re^{-i\theta}$.
Either $r=0$ (the root $z=0$), or divide by $re^{-i\theta}$: $re^{3i\theta}=e^{-i\pi/2}$.
Moduli: $r=1$. Arguments: $3\theta=-\frac\pi2+2k\pi$, so $\theta=-\frac\pi6+\frac{2k\pi}{3}$ for $k=0,1,2$.
$\theta=-30^\circ,\ 90^\circ,\ 210^\circ$ give $z=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac i2,\ i,\ -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac i2$ (matching the coordinates above).
Together with $z=0$ there are $3+1=4$ distinct roots.

useful_results: Equations of the form $z^m=c\,\bar z^{\,n}$ are solved in polar form: modulus equation $r^{m-n}=|c|$ (if $m\neq n$) and argument equation $(m+n)\theta=\arg c+2k\pi$, giving $m+n$ non-zero roots, plus $z=0$ when $m,n\ge1$.
$\frac{1-i}{1+i}=-i$ and $\frac{1+i}{1-i}=i$: memorise these two.
Always check $z=0$ separately when dividing by $z$ or $\bar z$.

questions.question: Let $A=\left\{\frac{1967+1686i\sin\theta}{7-3i\cos\theta}:\theta\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$. If $A$ contains exactly one positive integer $n$, then the value of $n$ is ____ [JEE-(Adv)2023]
questions.key_idea: $1967=281\cdot7$ and $1686=281\cdot6$: factor out $281$, then force the imaginary part to $0$.
solution: $A=\frac{1967+1686i\sin\theta}{7-3i\cos\theta}=\frac{281\left(7+6i\sin\theta\right)}{7-3i\cos\theta}$ (since $1967=281\times7$, $1686=281\times6$).
Rationalise: multiply by $\frac{7+3i\cos\theta}{7+3i\cos\theta}$: $A=\frac{281\left[(49-18\sin\theta\cos\theta)+i\left(21\cos\theta+42\sin\theta\right)\right]}{49+9\cos^2\theta}$.
For $A$ to be a positive integer it must be real: $\mathrm{Im}\,A=0\Rightarrow21\cos\theta+42\sin\theta=0$.
So $\tan\theta=-\frac12$, giving $\sin2\theta=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}=-\frac45$ and $\cos^2\theta=\frac{1}{1+\tan^2\theta}=\frac45$.
$\mathrm{Re}\,A=\frac{281\left(49-9\sin2\theta\right)}{49+9\cos^2\theta}=\frac{281\left(49+\frac{36}{5}\right)}{49+\frac{36}{5}}=281$.
The only real value in $A$ is $281$, a positive integer: $n=281$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Set $A=k$ and compare real and imaginary parts directly: $1967+1686i\sin\theta=k(7-3i\cos\theta)$ gives $k$ from the real part alone.
solution: If $A=k$ is a positive integer (real), then $1967+1686i\sin\theta=7k-3ki\cos\theta$.
Real parts: $7k=1967\Rightarrow k=281$.
Imaginary parts: $1686\sin\theta=-3k\cos\theta=-843\cos\theta$, i.e. $\tan\theta=-\frac12$ (so $\theta$ exists, e.g. $\theta=-\tan^{-1}\frac12$).
Check: $\sin\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt5},\cos\theta=\frac2{\sqrt5}$: $7-3i\cos\theta=7-\frac{6i}{\sqrt5}$ and $1967+1686i\sin\theta=1967-\frac{1686i}{\sqrt5}=281\left(7-\frac{6i}{\sqrt5}\right)$.
Hence the unique positive integer in $A$ is $n=281$.

useful_results: If a real number $k$ equals $\frac{p+iq}{r+is}$ then $p=kr$ and $q=ks$: compare parts instead of rationalising, and read $k$ off the part with no trigonometric function.
Look for common factors: $1967=7\times281$, $1686=6\times281$ (a hidden factor reveals the answer).
$\tan\theta=t\Rightarrow\sin2\theta=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $\cos^2\theta=\frac1{1+t^2}$.

concepts: Equation in $|z|$, $z$ and $\bar z$: separating real and imaginary parts

questions.question:
Let $z$ be a complex number satisfying $|z|^3+2z^2+4\bar z-8=0$, where $\bar z$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z$. Let the imaginary part of $z$ be non-zero.
Match each entry in List-I to the correct entries in List-II. [JEE-(Adv)2023]

List-I
(P) $|z|^2$ is equal to
(Q) $|z-\bar z|^2$ is equal to
(R) $|z|^2+|z+\bar z|^2$ is equal to
(S) $|z+1|^2$ is equal to

List-II
(1) $12$
(2) $4$
(3) $8$
(4) $10$
(5) $7$
questions.key_idea: Subtract the conjugate equation: $\left(z-\bar z\right)\left(z+\bar z-2\right)=0$, so $\mathrm{Re}\,z=1$ because $\mathrm{Im}\,z\neq0$.
solution: (1)$-$(2): $2\left(z^2-\bar z^2\right)+4(\bar z-z)=0\Rightarrow(z-\bar z)(z+\bar z)-2(z-\bar z)=0\Rightarrow(z-\bar z)(z+\bar z-2)=0$.
$z-\bar z\neq0$ (imaginary part non-zero), so $z+\bar z=2$, i.e. $x=1$ and $z=1+iy$.
$|z|=\sqrt{1+y^2}$, $z^2=1-y^2+2iy$, $\bar z=1-iy$. Substitute in (1): $\left(1+y^2\right)^{3/2}+2\left(1-y^2+2iy\right)+4(1-iy)-8=0$.
Imaginary parts cancel ($4iy-4iy=0$); real part: $\left(1+y^2\right)^{3/2}+2-2y^2+4-8=0\Rightarrow\left(1+y^2\right)^{3/2}-2\left(1+y^2\right)=0$.
$\left(1+y^2\right)\left(\sqrt{1+y^2}-2\right)=0\Rightarrow1+y^2=4$, so $y^2=3$.
So P-2, Q-1, R-3, S-5: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $z=x+iy$ and read the equation as two real equations: the imaginary part alone gives $x=1$.
solution: $z=x+iy$, $y\neq0$. Imaginary part of $|z|^3+2z^2+4\bar z-8$: $|z|^3$ and $-8$ are real, $2z^2$ contributes $4xy$ and $4\bar z$ contributes $-4y$.
So $4xy-4y=0\Rightarrow4y(x-1)=0\Rightarrow x=1$.
So P-2, Q-1, R-3, S-5: option (B).

useful_results: For an equation $F(z,\bar z,|z|)=0$ with real $|z|$: subtracting its conjugate kills $|z|$ and real constants and leaves $(z-\bar z)\times(\dots)$; with $z\neq\bar z$ the second factor gives a line.
$|z|^2=x^2+y^2$, $|z-\bar z|^2=4y^2$, $|z+\bar z|^2=4x^2$: convert every List-I quantity to $x,y$.
Check of the instance: $z=1+i\sqrt3$ gives $|z|^3=8$, $2z^2=-4+4\sqrt3 i$, $4\bar z=4-4\sqrt3i$: total $8-4+4-8=0$.

concepts: Roots of unity on a circle: product of distances from a point

questions.question: Let $A_1,A_2,A_3,\dots,A_8$ be the vertices of a regular octagon that lie on a circle of radius $2$. Let $P$ be a point on the circle and let $PA_i$ denote the distance between the points $P$ and $A_i$ for $i=1,2,\dots,8$. If $P$ varies over the circle, then the maximum value of the product $PA_1\cdot PA_2\cdot\dots\cdot PA_8$ is ____ [JEE-(Adv)2023]
questions.key_idea: The vertices are the roots of $z^8=2^8$, so $\prod(z-z_i)=z^8-2^8$ and the product of distances is $|z^8-2^8|\le2^9$.
solution: Place the circle at the origin: the vertices are $z_r=2e^{ir\pi/4}$, $r=0,1,\dots,7$ (the eight roots of $z^8=2^8$).
$PA_1\cdot PA_2\cdots PA_8=|z-z_1||z-z_2|\cdots|z-z_8|=\left|(z-z_1)(z-z_2)\cdots(z-z_8)\right|$ ... (1), where $z$ is the point $P$ with $|z|=2$.
Since the $z_r$ are all the roots of $z^8-2^8=0$: $z^8-2^8=(z-z_1)(z-z_2)\cdots(z-z_8)$.
So the product is $\left|z^8-2^8\right|=\left|z^8+(-2^8)\right|$.
By the triangle inequality $\left|z^8-2^8\right|\le|z|^8+2^8=2^8+2^8=2^9$.
Equality holds when $z^8=-2^8$, i.e. $P$ at the midpoint of an arc between two adjacent vertices (such $z$ exist on $|z|=2$).
Maximum product $=2^9=512$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the vertices as z_r = 2e^{i r pi/8}, r=0..7; the vertices of a regular octagon are at angles 2 pi r/8 = r pi/4 (r pi/8 would give a 16-gon and does not satisfy z^8 = 2^8). Corrected to e^{i r pi/4}. The rest of the working and the answer 512 are the PDF's.

alternate_solutions.idea: Trigonometry: each distance is $4\left|\sin\frac{\phi-\phi_r}{2}\right|$ and $\prod_{r=0}^{7}\sin\left(x+\frac{r\pi}{8}\right)=\frac{\sin8x}{2^7}$.
solution: Let $P=2e^{i\phi}$ and $A_r=2e^{i\pi r/4}$. The chord is $PA_r=2\cdot2\left|\sin\frac{\phi-\pi r/4}{2}\right|=4\left|\sin\left(\frac\phi2-\frac{r\pi}{8}\right)\right|$.
The product is $4^8\prod_{r=0}^{7}\left|\sin\left(x-\frac{r\pi}{8}\right)\right|$ with $x=\frac\phi2$.
Use $\prod_{r=0}^{n-1}\sin\left(x+\frac{r\pi}{n}\right)=\frac{\sin nx}{2^{n-1}}$ with $n=8$ (the terms $x-\frac{r\pi}8$ are the same angles mod $\pi$ up to sign).
So the product is $4^8\cdot\frac{|\sin8x|}{2^7}=\frac{65536}{128}|\sin4\phi|=512\,|\sin4\phi|$.
The maximum is $512$ (when $\sin4\phi=\pm1$).

useful_results: For the $n$th roots of $c$: $\prod_k(z-z_k)=z^n-c$, so the product of distances from a point $z$ to the vertices of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in $|z|=R$ is $|z^n-R^n|\in\left[0,2R^n\right]$.
Max is $2R^n$ (at arc midpoints) and min $0$ (at a vertex). Here $R=2,n=8$: $2\cdot2^8=512$.
The same identity gives $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}|1-\omega^k|=n$ (put $z=R=1$, divide by $z-1$) for the chords from one vertex.

questions.question: Let $S=\left\{a+b\sqrt2:a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}$, $T_1=\left\{\left(-1+\sqrt2\right)^n:n\in\mathbb{N}\right\}$ and $T_2=\left\{\left(1+\sqrt2\right)^n:n\in\mathbb{N}\right\}$. Then which of the following statements is(are) TRUE? [JEE-(Adv)2024]
options: $\mathbb{Z}\cup T_1\cup T_2=S$ (as printed in the paper; the key reads this as $\subset S$)
For any given $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\cos\left(\pi\left(a+b\sqrt2\right)\right)+i\sin\left(\pi\left(a+b\sqrt2\right)\right)\in\mathbb{Z}$ if and only if $b=0$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$.
questions.answer: (C, D)  [the key (A, C, D) holds only if (A) is read as $\mathbb{Z}\cup T_1\cup T_2\subset S$]
questions.key_idea: $e^{i\pi(a+b\sqrt2)}$ is an integer only if its sine vanishes, i.e. $a+b\sqrt2\in\mathbb{Z}$, which by irrationality of $\sqrt2$ means $b=0$.
solution: $T_1$: $\left(-1+\sqrt2\right)^n=\frac{1}{\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^n}$, so $\left(T_1\right)_{\max}=\frac1{\sqrt2+1}\approx0.4142$ (at $n=1$) and the values tend to $0$.
Hence terms of $T_1$ lie in $\left(0,\frac1{2024}\right)$ for large $n$, so $T_1\cap\left(0,\frac1{2024}\right)\neq\phi$ and (B) is false.
$T_2$: $\left(1+\sqrt2\right)^n$ has minimum $1+\sqrt2\approx2.414$ and tends to $\infty$, so it has terms greater than $2024$: (C) is true.
(D) $\cos\pi(a+b\sqrt2)+i\sin\pi(a+b\sqrt2)=e^{i\pi(a+b\sqrt2)}$ is an integer only if its imaginary part is $0$: $\sin\pi\left(a+b\sqrt2\right)=0$.
Then $\pi\left(a+b\sqrt2\right)=m\pi$, so $a+b\sqrt2=m\in\mathbb{Z}$; since $\sqrt2$ is irrational this forces $b=0$. Conversely, $b=0$ gives $e^{i\pi a}=\pm1\in\mathbb{Z}$. So (D) is true.
(A) Every element of $\mathbb{Z}$, $T_1$ and $T_2$ is of the form $a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ (powers of $\pm1+\sqrt2$ stay in $S$), hence $\mathbb{Z}\cup T_1\cup T_2\subset S$ is true.

But equality fails as printed: $\sqrt2\in S$ is not an integer and equals no $\left(\pm1+\sqrt2\right)^n$ (every element $p+q\sqrt2$ of $T_1\cup T_2$ has $p^2-2q^2=\pm1$, while $\sqrt2=0+1\cdot\sqrt2$ has $0-2=-2$). So the statement with '$=$' is false; the key's (A) is for '$\subset$'.
questions.correction_note: Option (A) is printed as 'Z union T1 union T2 = S' in the paper, but the PDF's own solution proves only 'subset of S' (and the key lists A). With equality, (A) is false (for example sqrt2 is in S but in none of Z, T1, T2), so the answer for the question as printed is (C, D); the key (A, C, D) is right only if (A) reads 'subset'. Reported in the run report.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the unit $u=1+\sqrt2$ with $u^{-1}=\sqrt2-1$: $T_2=\{u^n\}$, $T_1=\{u^{-n}\}$; (B), (C) follow from $u>1$.
solution: $\left(\sqrt2-1\right)\left(\sqrt2+1\right)=1$, so with $u=1+\sqrt2>1$: $T_2=\{u^n:n\ge1\}$ and $T_1=\{u^{-n}:n\ge1\}$.
$u>1$ implies $u^n\to\infty$ and $u^{-n}\to0^{+}$, so $T_2\cap(2024,\infty)\neq\phi$ (C true) and $T_1$ has terms below $\frac1{2024}$, so $T_1\cap\left(0,\frac1{2024}\right)\neq\phi$ (B false).
For (D): $e^{i\pi x}\in\mathbb{Z}$ means $e^{i\pi x}=\pm1$ (it has modulus $1$), i.e. $x\in\mathbb{Z}$; with $x=a+b\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt2\notin\mathbb{Q}$ this means $b=0$, and for $b=0$ it holds.
So (C) and (D) are true and (B) false; (A) holds only as a subset relation.

useful_results: $u=1+\sqrt2$ is a unit of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ ($u\cdot\left(\sqrt2-1\right)=1$): all powers $u^{\pm n}$ stay in $a+b\sqrt2$ form, with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$; $u^n=p_n+q_n\sqrt2$ with $\left(p_n,q_n\right)$ from $p_{n+1}=p_n+2q_n,\ q_{n+1}=p_n+q_n$.
$e^{i\pi x}$ is real iff $x\in\mathbb{Z}$ (value $\pm1$); it is an integer iff $x\in\mathbb{Z}$. With irrational $\sqrt2$, $a+b\sqrt2\in\mathbb{Z}\iff b=0$.
Read inclusion symbols carefully: '$\cup$ of subsets $=S$' needs every element of $S$ covered; here $\sqrt2\in S$ is not covered by $\mathbb Z\cup T_1\cup T_2$.

questions.question: Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Let $z_1=1+2i$ and $z_2=3i$ be two complex numbers, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Let $S=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}:|x+iy-z_1|=2|x+iy-z_2|\right\}$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE? [JEE-(Adv)2025]
questions.key_idea: Square $|z-z_1|=2|z-z_2|$ and complete the squares: it is an Apollonius circle.
solution: This is a circle with centre $\left(-\frac13,\frac{10}{3}\right)$.
Radius $=\sqrt{\frac19+\frac{100}{9}-\frac{31}{3}}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{9}}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$.
So (A) and (D) are true; (B) and (C) are false.

questions.question: For a non-zero complex number $z$, let $\arg(z)$ denote the principal argument of $z$, with $-\pi<\arg(z)\le\pi$. Let $\omega$ be the cube root of unity for which $0<\arg(\omega)<\pi$. Let $\alpha=\arg\left(\sum_{n=1}^{2025}(-\omega)^n\right)$. Then the value of $\frac{3\alpha}{\pi}$ is ____ [JEE-(Adv)2025]
questions.key_idea: The sum is a geometric series with ratio $-\omega$ and $\omega^{2025}=1$, which gives $2\omega^2$.
solution: $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ (the cube root of unity with $0<\arg\omega<\pi$).
$\sum_{n=1}^{2025}(-\omega)^n=-\omega+\omega^2-\omega^3+\omega^4-\dots-\omega^{2025}$, a geometric series with first term $-\omega$, ratio $-\omega$ and $2025$ terms.
Sum $=\frac{(-\omega)\left(1-(-\omega)^{2025}\right)}{1-(-\omega)}=\frac{(-\omega)\left(1+\omega^{2025}\right)}{1+\omega}$ (as $2025$ is odd).
$2025$ is a multiple of $3$, so $\omega^{2025}=1$; also $1+\omega=-\omega^2$. Hence sum $=\frac{-\omega\cdot2}{-\omega^2}=\frac2\omega=2\omega^2$.
$2\omega^2=2e^{4\pi i/3}$; its principal argument is $\frac{4\pi}{3}-2\pi=-\frac{2\pi}{3}$, so $\alpha=-\frac{2\pi}3$.
$\frac{3\alpha}{\pi}=-2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $-\omega=e^{-i\pi/3}$ is a primitive 6th root of unity, so the terms repeat with period $6$ and every full period sums to $0$.
solution: $-\omega=e^{i\pi}e^{2\pi i/3}=e^{5\pi i/3}=e^{-i\pi/3}$; it is a primitive 6th root of unity, so $(-\omega)^{n+6}=(-\omega)^n$.
$1+\left(-\omega\right)+\dots+(-\omega)^5=0$, so any $6$ consecutive terms sum to $0$.
$2025=6\cdot337+3$: the first $2022$ terms cancel, leaving $(-\omega)^{2023}+(-\omega)^{2024}+(-\omega)^{2025}$, equal to $(-\omega)^1+(-\omega)^2+(-\omega)^3$ by periodicity.
$=e^{-i\pi/3}+e^{-2i\pi/3}+e^{-i\pi}=\left(\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}2i\right)+\left(-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}2i\right)-1=-1-\sqrt3i=2e^{-2\pi i/3}$.
So $\alpha=-\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{3\alpha}\pi=-2$.

useful_results: $\sum_{n=1}^{N}\rho^n=\rho\,\frac{1-\rho^N}{1-\rho}$ for $\rho\neq1$; for a root of unity $\rho$ of order $m$, $m$ consecutive terms sum to $0$, so only $N\bmod m$ terms survive.
$-\omega=e^{-i\pi/3}$ and $-\omega^2=e^{i\pi/3}$ are the primitive 6th roots of unity; $1+\omega=-\omega^2$, $1+\omega^2=-\omega$.
Principal argument must be reduced into $(-\pi,\pi]$: $\arg\left(2e^{4\pi i/3}\right)=-\frac{2\pi}3$, not $\frac{4\pi}3$.

questions.question: Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers and let $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Consider the matrices $S=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Let $a,b,c,d$ be real numbers such that $ST=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. Let $H=\{x+iy:x,y\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }y>0\}$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE: [JEE-(Adv)2026]
options: If $m$ is an integer greater than $2$ such that $(ST)^2=(ST)^m$, then $m$ is an integer multiple of $8$
questions.key_idea: $ST=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ has $(ST)^3=-I$ and acts as $z\mapsto-\frac1{z+1}$, with fixed point $\omega$ and determinant $1>0$.
solution: $ST=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $a=0,\ b=-1,\ c=1,\ d=1$.
(A) $\frac{b+ia}{d+ic}=\frac{-1}{1+i}=\frac{-1}{1+i}\cdot\frac{1-i}{1-i}=\frac{i-1}{2}\neq i$: incorrect.
(B) $\frac{a\omega+b}{c\omega+d}=\frac{-1}{\omega+1}=\frac{-1}{-\omega^2}=\frac1{\omega^2}=\omega$ (since $1+\omega=-\omega^2$ and $\omega^3=1$): correct.
(C) $(ST)^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
$(ST)^3=(ST)^2(ST)=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}=-I$, hence $(ST)^6=I$ and the order of $ST$ is $6$.
$(ST)^2=(ST)^m\iff(ST)^{m-2}=I\iff6\mid(m-2)$, i.e. $m=6\lambda+2$. Then $m=8$ works but $m=14$ also works and is not a multiple of $8$: (C) is incorrect.
Its imaginary part is $\frac{y}{(x+1)^2+y^2}>0$ because $y>0$, so the image lies in $H$: (D) is correct. Answer: (B), (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Möbius viewpoint: $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ acts as $z\mapsto\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$; $\mathrm{Im}\,\frac{az+b}{cz+d}=\frac{(ad-bc)\,\mathrm{Im}z}{|cz+d|^2}$ and fixed points solve $cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$.
solution: For $ST=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$: $\det=ad-bc=0\cdot1-(-1)(1)=1>0$.
(D) $\mathrm{Im}\frac{az+b}{cz+d}=\frac{(ad-bc)\,y}{|cz+d|^2}=\frac{y}{|z+1|^2}>0$ for $y>0$ (verified by multiplying numerator and denominator by $\overline{cz+d}$): (D) true.
(B) Fixed points: $z=\frac{-1}{z+1}\iff z^2+z+1=0\iff z=\omega,\ \bar\omega$. So $\omega$ is fixed: (B) true.

(C) The map $z\mapsto\frac{-1}{z+1}$ has order $3$ (the matrix has $(ST)^3=-I$, a scalar), but as a matrix $(ST)^k=(ST)^{k-2}\cdot(ST)^2$ needs $(ST)^{m-2}=I$ exactly, not $\pm I$; $(ST)^3=-I\neq I$, so $6\mid m-2$: $m=8,14,20,\dots$, and $14$ is not a multiple of $8$: (C) false.
(A) $\frac{b+ia}{d+ic}=\frac{-1}{1+i}=\frac{-1+i}{2}\neq i$: false. So (B), (D).

useful_results: For a real matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ acting by $z\mapsto\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$: $\mathrm{Im}\,M(z)=\frac{\det M\cdot\mathrm{Im}\,z}{|cz+d|^2}$, so $\det M>0$ preserves the upper half-plane (and $\det M<0$ swaps it with the lower one).

Composition of Möbius maps corresponds to matrix multiplication; scalar matrices act as the identity, so the matrix order can be twice the order of the map ($(ST)^3=-I$: map order $3$, matrix order $6$).
Fixed points of $z\mapsto\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$ satisfy $cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$; here $z^2+z+1=0$, i.e. $z=\omega,\bar\omega$ (order-$3$ rotation of the half-plane).

(P) If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2+x+1=0$, then the quadratic equation with roots $\frac{1}{(\alpha+1)^{2026}}$ and $\frac{1}{(\beta+1)^{2026}}$ is
(Q) If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2+x+1=0$, then the quadratic equation with roots $\frac{1}{(\alpha+1)^{2027}}$ and $\frac{1}{(\beta+1)^{2027}}$ is
(R) If $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2-x+1=0$, then the value of $\frac{1}{(\gamma-1)^{2026}}+\frac{1}{(\delta-1)^{2026}}$ is
(S) If $p$ and $r$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2+x-1=0$, then the value of $\frac{1}{(p+1)^3}+\frac{1}{(r+1)^3}$ is

List-II
(1) $x^2+x+1=0$
(2) $x^2-x+1=0$
(3) $x^2+x-1=0$
(4) $-1$

questions.key_idea: For roots of $x^2+x+1=0$, $\alpha+1=-\alpha^2$ so $\frac1{\alpha+1}=-\alpha$; reduce the huge exponents with $\omega^3=1$.
solution: Let $\alpha=\omega,\ \beta=\omega^2$ (roots of $x^2+x+1=0$). Then $1+\omega=-\omega^2$ and $1+\omega^2=-\omega$.
(P) $\frac1{(\alpha+1)^{2026}}=\frac{1}{\left(-\omega^2\right)^{2026}}=\frac1{\omega^{4052}}=\frac1{\omega^2}=\omega$ (as $4052\equiv2\pmod3$).
$\frac1{(\beta+1)^{2026}}=\frac1{(-\omega)^{2026}}=\frac1{\omega^{2026}}=\frac1\omega=\omega^2$ (as $2026\equiv1$). The roots are $\omega,\omega^2$: the equation is $x^2+x+1=0$ $\to$ (1).

(Q) $\frac1{(\alpha+1)^{2027}}=\frac1{\left(-\omega^2\right)^{2027}}=-\frac1{\omega^{4054}}=-\frac1\omega=-\omega^2$, and $\frac1{(\beta+1)^{2027}}=\frac1{(-\omega)^{2027}}=-\frac1{\omega^{2027}}=-\frac1{\omega^2}=-\omega$.
Roots $-\omega,-\omega^2$: sum $=-(\omega+\omega^2)=1$, product $=\omega^3=1$: the equation is $x^2-x+1=0$ $\to$ (2).
(R) The roots of $x^2-x+1=0$ are $\gamma=-\omega^2$ and $\delta=-\omega$ (sum $1$, product $1$). Then $\gamma-1=-\omega^2-1=\omega$ and $\delta-1=-\omega-1=\omega^2$.
$\frac1{(\gamma-1)^{2026}}=\omega^{-2026}=\omega^{-1}=\omega^2$ and $\frac1{(\delta-1)^{2026}}=\omega^{-4052}=\omega^{-2}=\omega$. The sum is $\omega+\omega^2=-1$ $\to$ (4).
So P-1, Q-2, R-4, S-5: option (C).
questions.correction_note: (R) PDF takes gamma - 1 = -w^2 and writes 1/(gamma-1)^2026 = 1/(-w^2)^2026 = w; in fact gamma = -w^2 gives gamma - 1 = w (not -w^2). The PDF's two terms (w and w^2) have the right sum -1 only by luck; the correct terms are w^2 and w. (S) PDF stops after p^3 + r^3 = -4 and 'S -> 5' without evaluating the numerator and denominator of the combined fraction (numerator 4, denominator -1); completed with u = p+1, v = r+1. Answer key C is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Each root satisfies its quadratic, which turns $\frac1{\text{root}\pm1}$ into a simple expression: $\frac1{\alpha+1}=-\alpha$, $\frac1{\gamma-1}=\gamma^{-2}$, $\frac1{p+1}=p$.
solution: (P),(Q) $\alpha^2+\alpha+1=0\Rightarrow\alpha(\alpha+1)=-1$ hence $\frac1{\alpha+1}=-\alpha$ (similarly for $\beta$). So the new roots are $(-\alpha)^n,(-\beta)^n$.

$n=2026$: $\alpha^{2026}=\alpha$ and $\beta^{2026}=\beta$ (as $\alpha^3=1$, $2026\equiv1$): same roots, so $x^2+x+1=0$ (1). $n=2027$: $-\alpha^{2027}=-\alpha^2=-\beta$ and $-\beta^{2027}=-\alpha$: roots $-\alpha,-\beta$, giving $x^2-x+1=0$ (2).

(R) $\gamma^2-\gamma+1=0\Rightarrow\gamma-1=\gamma^2$, so $\frac1{(\gamma-1)^{2026}}=\gamma^{-4052}$. $\gamma$ has order $6$ and $4052\equiv2\pmod6$, so the term is $\gamma^{-2}$; likewise $\delta^{-2}$. With $\gamma=e^{i\pi/3}$, $\delta=\bar\gamma$: $e^{-2\pi i/3}+e^{2\pi i/3}=-1$ (4).
(S) $p^2+p-1=0\Rightarrow p(p+1)=1\Rightarrow\frac1{p+1}=p$. So the expression is $p^3+r^3=(p+r)^3-3pr(p+r)=-1-3(-1)(-1)=-4$ (5).
So P-1, Q-2, R-4, S-5: option (C).

useful_results: If $x$ satisfies $x^2+bx+c=0$, then $x(x+b)=-c$, so $\frac{1}{x+b}=-\frac xc$: for $x^2+x+1$: $\frac1{x+1}=-x$; for $x^2+x-1$: $\frac1{x+1}=x$. Remove the denominators before taking powers.
Powers of cube roots of unity depend on the exponent mod $3$ (primitive 6th roots: mod $6$); $(-\omega)^n$ has period $6$.
A new quadratic with roots $f(\alpha),f(\beta)$: use the sum and product ($x^2-(\text{sum})x+\text{product}$); for $x^2-x+1=0$ the roots are $-\omega,-\omega^2$, i.e. $e^{\pm i\pi/3}$.
